newsitem.title: USA: Republicans attack Clinton's Haiti policy.
newsitem.headline: Republicans attack Clinton's Haiti policy.

text.p: House Republicans on Friday renewed their attacks on administration actions in Haiti but Democrats said they were only trying to discredit one of President Bill Clinton's biggest foreign policy successes.

"The Clinton administration has spent more than $2 billion to support a government that has tolerated thugs who murder its political opponents," Benjamin Gilman, the New York Republican who chairs the House of Representatives International Relations Committee, said at a hearing on last month's murders of two Haitian opposition leaders.

Gilman and Indiana Republican Dan Burton accused the administration of covering up by refusing to let the committee see about 50 documents about administration policy in Haiti. The papers cover the period since Clinton sent U.S. troops in 1994 to restore the government of President Jean-Bertrand Aristide, overthrown by a military coup three years earlier.
The White House invoked executive privilege on Wednesday in refusing to hand over the documents.
"I believe there was a deliberate attempt to cover up," Burton said. He said an administration official had lied during previous hearings on a 1995 political murder.
Committee Democrats called the attacks part of an effort to help Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole.

"Haiti is clearly a success. The president took the risk. This hearing is about trying to deny what is happening in Haiti," Connecticut Democrat Sam Gejdenson said. "This is pure political posturing," Florida Democrat Alcee Hastings said.
"No president has done more to help Haitians determine their own peaceful destiny than Bill Clinton," Michigan Democrat John Conyers said.

William Swing, U.S. ambassador to Haiti, and Joseph Sullivan, the State Department's special Haiti coordinator, acknowledged that Haiti faced enormous problems but said it had made progress since the U.S. intervention.

"It is clear that the level of political violence in Haiti has declined significantly," Sullivan said. "We firmly believe that it is in our national interest to support President (Rene) Preval as he continues work to build Haitian democracy and its institutions."
"I believe the trend line is positive," Swing said. But he said there was evidence that members of Preval's presidential security unit had been involved in the recent murders.
Preval has suspended the director and deputy director of the unit pending an investigation. The United States sent 40 security agents to Haiti at Preval's request to help reorganize the unit.
